claim: Sensory systems modulate neuronal responses to stimuli based on statistical context.
source: Sensory systems must account for both contextual factors and prior experience to adaptively engage with the dynamic external environment. In the central auditory system, neurons modulate their responses to sounds based on statistical context.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general principle of sensory system function.

claim: Response modulations in the auditory system can be understood through a hierarchical predictive coding lens.
source: These response modulations can be understood through a hierarchical predictive coding lens: responses to repeated stimuli are progressively decreased, in a process known as repetition suppression, whereas unexpected stimuli produce a prediction error signal.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework stated in the abstract for interpreting the experimental findings.

claim: Repetition suppression is characterized by progressively decreased responses to repeated stimuli.
source: responses to repeated stimuli are progressively decreased, in a process known as repetition suppression
evidence: This is a definition provided in the abstract.

claim: Unexpected stimuli produce a prediction error signal.
source: whereas unexpected stimuli produce a prediction error signal.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of predictive coding in the abstract.

claim: Prediction error incrementally increases along the auditory hierarchy from the inferior colliculus to the auditory cortex.
source: Prediction error incrementally increases along the auditory hierarchy from the inferior colliculus (IC) to the auditory cortex (AC), suggesting that these regions may engage in hierarchical predictive coding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an observation that motivates the study.

claim: The auditory cortex sends massive descending projections to subcortical structures.
source: A potential substrate for top-down predictive cues is the massive set of descending projections from the AC to subcortical structures
evidence: This is stated as anatomical background in the abstract.

claim: The role of descending projections from auditory cortex in predictive processing has never been directly assessed prior to this study.
source: although the role of this system in predictive processing has never been directly assessed.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Optogenetic inactivation of the auditory cortico-collicular feedback in awake mice leads to a decrease in prediction error in IC.
source: Inactivation of the cortico-collicular pathway led to a decrease in prediction error in IC.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Repetition suppression is unaffected by cortico-collicular inactivation.
source: Repetition suppression was unaffected by cortico-collicular inactivation, suggesting that this metric may reflect fatigue of bottom-up sensory inputs rather than predictive processing.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Repetition suppression may reflect fatigue of bottom-up sensory inputs rather than predictive processing.
source: Repetition suppression was unaffected by cortico-collicular inactivation, suggesting that this metric may reflect fatigue of bottom-up sensory inputs rather than predictive processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental finding that repetition suppression is unaffected by inactivation.

claim: Populations of IC units exhibit repetition enhancement, a sequential increase in firing with stimulus repetition.
source: We also discovered populations of IC units that exhibit repetition enhancement, a sequential increase in firing with stimulus repetition.
evidence: This is a novel finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: Cortico-collicular inactivation leads to a decrease in repetition enhancement in the central nucleus of IC.
source: Cortico-collicular inactivation led to a decrease in repetition enhancement in the central nucleus of IC, suggesting that it is a top-down phenomenon.
evidence: This is an experimental finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3G.

claim: Repetition enhancement in the central nucleus of IC is a top-down phenomenon.
source: Cortico-collicular inactivation led to a decrease in repetition enhancement in the central nucleus of IC, suggesting that it is a top-down phenomenon.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental finding that repetition enhancement decreases with cortical inactivation.

claim: Negative prediction error is a stronger response to a tone in a predictable rather than unpredictable sequence.
source: Negative prediction error, a stronger response to a tone in a predictable rather than unpredictable sequence, was suppressed in shell IC units during cortico-collicular inactivation.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the abstract.

claim: Negative prediction error is suppressed in shell IC units during cortico-collicular inactivation.
source: Negative prediction error, a stronger response to a tone in a predictable rather than unpredictable sequence, was suppressed in shell IC units during cortico-collicular inactivation.
evidence: This is an experimental finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3H.

claim: Changes in predictive coding metrics arise from bidirectional modulations in the response to the standard and deviant contexts.
source: These changes in predictive coding metrics arose from bidirectional modulations in the response to the standard and deviant contexts, such that the units in IC responded more similarly to each context in the absence of cortical input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: In the absence of cortical input, IC units respond more similarly to standard and deviant contexts.
source: such that the units in IC responded more similarly to each context in the absence of cortical input.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the bidirectional modulation findings.

claim: Metrics of predictive coding and deviance detection differ depending on the anesthetic state of the animal.
source: We found that metrics of predictive coding and deviance detection differ depending on the anesthetic state of the animal
evidence: This is an experimental finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Negative prediction error emerges in the central IC in the awake state.
source: with negative prediction error emerging in the central IC and repetition enhancement and prediction error being more prevalent in the absence of anesthesia.
evidence: This is an experimental finding comparing awake and anesthetized states, supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Repetition enhancement and prediction error are more prevalent in the absence of anesthesia.
source: with negative prediction error emerging in the central IC and repetition enhancement and prediction error being more prevalent in the absence of anesthesia.
evidence: This is an experimental finding comparing awake and anesthetized states, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The auditory cortex provides cues about the statistical context of sound to subcortical brain regions via direct feedback.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate that the AC provides cues about the statistical context of sound to subcortical brain regions via direct feedback, regulating processing of both prediction and repetition.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Neurons in select regions of the central auditory system are sensitive to statistical context.
source: Neurons in select regions of the central auditory system are sensitive to statistical context, responding more strongly to a tone when it is presented rarely (a 'deviant') than when it is commonplace (a 'standard') (Ulanovsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature.

claim: Stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA) is prevalent in the auditory cortex.
source: This phenomenon, known as stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA), is prevalent in the auditory cortex (AC) (Natan et al., 2015; Ulanovsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature.

claim: Weaker SSA is present in the inferior colliculus and medial geniculate body compared to auditory cortex.
source: Weaker SSA is present in regions peripheral to the AC, including the auditory midbrain, or inferior colliculus (IC), and the auditory thalamus, or medial geniculate body (MGB) (Anderson et al., 2009; Antunes et al., 2010; Duque and Malmierca, 2015; Malmierca et al., 2009; Taaseh et al., 2011; Ulanovsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature.

claim: Subdivisions in IC and MGB that receive descending projections from AC exhibit relatively higher SSA levels than their lemniscal counterparts.
source: Subdivisions in IC and MGB that receive descending projections from AC exhibit relatively higher SSA levels than their lemniscal counterparts (Antunes et al., 2010; Duque et al., 2012)
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature.

claim: SSA may be generated de novo in AC and subsequently broadcast to subcortical structures via corticofugal projections.
source: suggesting that SSA may be generated de novo in AC and subsequently broadcast to subcortical structures via corticofugal projections (Nelken and Ulanovsky, 2007).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature cited in the introduction.

claim: Silencing of AC through cooling modulates, but does not abolish, SSA in IC and MGB of anesthetized rats.
source: Silencing of AC through cooling, however, has been shown to modulate, but not abolish, SSA in IC and MGB of anesthetized rats (Anderson and Malmierca, 2013; Antunes and Malmierca, 2011).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature.

claim: Recent studies have decomposed the traditional SSA index into repetition suppression and prediction error using additional control tone sequences.
source: Recent studies have implemented additional control tone sequences to further decompose the traditional SSA index into two distinct underlying processes: repetition suppression and prediction error (Harms et al., 2014; Parras et al., 2017; Ruhnau et al., 2012).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature.

claim: Hierarchical predictive coding posits that prediction errors signal the mismatch between predictions and actual sensory input.
source: Hierarchical predictive coding posits that prediction errors signal the mismatch between predictions, formed based on prior experience with repeated presentations of the standard, and actual sensory input in the presence of a deviant (Friston, 2009; Friston and Kiebel, 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework cited from previous literature.

claim: Predictions are generated at higher levels of the sensory hierarchy and broadcast to lower stations to minimize processing of redundant input and maximize coding efficiency.
source: These predictions are generated at higher levels of the sensory hierarchy and broadcast to lower stations to minimize processing of redundant input and maximize coding efficiency (Friston, 2009; Friston and Kiebel, 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework cited from previous literature.

claim: Prediction error has been proposed to underlie true deviance detection.
source: Prediction error has been proposed to underlie true deviance detection, while repetition suppression is thought to potentially reflect synaptic depression (Parras et al., 2017; Taaseh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature cited in the introduction.

claim: Repetition suppression is thought to potentially reflect synaptic depression.
source: Prediction error has been proposed to underlie true deviance detection, while repetition suppression is thought to potentially reflect synaptic depression (Parras et al., 2017; Taaseh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature cited in the introduction.

claim: Prediction error is more prevalent in regions of IC and MGB that receive cortical feedback.
source: Prediction error increases along the auditory hierarchy and is more prevalent in regions of IC and MGB that receive cortical feedback (Parras et al., 2017)
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature.

claim: IC and MGB may engage in hierarchical predictive coding, with AC potentially providing predictive cues.
source: suggesting that these subcortical regions may engage in hierarchical predictive coding, with AC potentially providing predictive cues to IC and MGB.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous literature that motivates the current study.

claim: How feedback projections from AC shape predictive processing in subcortical targets has never been directly assessed prior to this study.
source: However, how feedback projections from AC shape predictive processing in subcortical targets has never been directly assessed.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Virtually all models of hierarchical predictive coding to date have focused on intracortical connections.
source: In fact, virtually all models of hierarchical predictive coding to date have focused on intracortical connections, with the massive system of descending corticofugal projections remaining unexplored (Asilador and Llano, 2020; Bastos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature.

claim: The massive system of descending corticofugal projections has remained unexplored in predictive coding models.
source: In fact, virtually all models of hierarchical predictive coding to date have focused on intracortical connections, with the massive system of descending corticofugal projections remaining unexplored (Asilador and Llano, 2020; Bastos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The inferior colliculus is the first station in the auditory system in which prediction error is found.
source: Here, we investigated how inputs from AC to IC, the first station in the auditory system in which prediction error is found, shape metrics associated with predictive coding and deviance detection (Parras et al., 2017).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature.

claim: A Cre/FLEX viral injection strategy was used to selectively express ArchT in cortico-collicular neurons.
source: We used a Cre/FLEX viral injection strategy to selectively express the inhibitory opsin, ArchT, in cortico-collicular neurons of four mice by injecting a retroAAV-Cre-GFP construct into IC and an AAV9-FLEX-ArchT-tdTomato construct into AC (Figure 1A, left).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by Figure 1A.

claim: The retroAAV-Cre-GFP construct is transported in a retrograde fashion and expressed in neurons that project to IC.
source: The retroAAV-Cre-GFP construct is transported in a retrograde fashion and expressed in neurons that project to IC (Blackwell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological description citing previous work.

claim: ArchT is a light-driven outward proton pump that mediates rapid, reversible inactivation of neurons.
source: In the presence of green light, ArchT, a light-driven outward proton pump, mediates rapid, reversible inactivation of the neurons in which it is expressed (Han et al., 2011).
evidence: This is background information about the optogenetic tool cited from previous literature.

claim: Expression of the retroAAV-Cre-GFP construct at the injection site is restricted to the inferior colliculus.
source: Examination of fixed tissue from injected mice revealed that expression of the retroAAV-Cre-GFP construct was restricted to IC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, top left).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Somatic expression of GFP is restricted to layer 5 and deep layer 6 of AC, which contain cortico-collicular cell bodies.
source: Somatic expression of GFP (indicating the presence of Cre) was restricted to layer 5 and deep layer 6 of AC, which contain cortico-collicular cell bodies, and was broadly distributed throughout the rostro-caudal extent of AC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, right) (Bajo et al., 2007; Schofield, 2009; Yudintsev et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and cited literature.

claim: Expression of tdTomato is found in the soma and processes of neurons in layers 5 and 6, with additional apical dendritic labeling observed in the upper cortical layers.
source: Expression of tdTomato was found in the soma and processes of neurons in layers 5 and 6, with additional apical dendritic labeling observed in the upper cortical layers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, right).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The laminar expression of tdTomato is consistent with previous studies and suggests that AAV9-FLEX-ArchT-tdTomato expression is Cre-dependent.
source: The laminar expression of tdTomato is consistent with previous studies and suggests that AAV9-FLEX-ArchT-tdTomato expression is Cre-dependent and not due to nonspecific labeling (Blackwell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observation citing previous work.

claim: Axons and terminals labeled with tdTomato are distributed in IC in a manner matching the known projection pattern of the cortico-collicular pathway.
source: Axons and terminals labeled with tdTomato were distributed in IC in a manner matching the known projection pattern of this pathway, with dense, 'patchy' labeling in shell regions of IC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, bottom left) (Herbert et al., 1991; Lesicko et al., 2016; Saldaña et al., 1996; Torii et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and cited literature.

claim: The viral injection strategy leads to selective transfection of cortico-collicular neurons.
source: These data confirm that our viral injection strategy leads to selective transfection of cortico-collicular neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the histological observations.

claim: Laser-induced inactivation led to a mean ~60% reduction in firing rate at baseline in putative cortico-collicular units.
source: In these putative cortico-collicular units, laser-induced inactivation led to a mean ~60% reduction in firing rate at baseline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, left; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, top; Table 1; p=1.9e-06, Wilcoxon signed-rank test)
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D, and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Laser-induced inactivation led to an average ~45% reduction in firing during presentation of pure tone stimuli in putative cortico-collicular units.
source: and an average ~45% reduction in firing during presentation of pure tone stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, right; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, bottom; Table 1; p=1.9e-06, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D, and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: The optogenetic parameters significantly suppress cortico-collicular units.
source: These results indicate that our optogenetic parameters significantly suppress cortico-collicular units.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings of reduced firing rates.

claim: Shell and central regions of IC differ in their tuning, degree of adaptation, and amount of input from AC.
source: Shell and central regions of IC differ in their tuning, degree of adaptation, and amount of input from AC, and may also play distinct roles in predictive processing (Aitkin et al., 1975; Bajo et al., 2007; Blackwell et al., 2020; Duque et al., 2012; Herbert et al., 1991; Stebbings et al., 2014; Syka et al., 2000).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature.

claim: Shell IC neurons tend to have broader frequency tuning (low sparseness) than central IC neurons.
source: shell IC neurons tend to have broader frequency tuning (low sparseness) than central IC neurons, and the central IC is characterized by a highly stereotyped tonotopic gradient with depth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; Aitkin et al., 1975; Chen et al., 2012; Malmierca et al., 2008; Stiebler and Ehret, 1985; Syka et al., 2000).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The central IC is characterized by a highly stereotyped tonotopic gradient with depth.
source: shell IC neurons tend to have broader frequency tuning (low sparseness) than central IC neurons, and the central IC is characterized by a highly stereotyped tonotopic gradient with depth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; Aitkin et al., 1975; Chen et al., 2012; Malmierca et al., 2008; Stiebler and Ehret, 1985; Syka et al., 2000).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Clustering analysis using mean sparsity and variation in best frequency with depth was used to determine whether recording sites were from the central nucleus or shell regions of IC.
source: Similar to previously established procedures used in human and monkey IC research, we performed clustering analysis using the mean sparsity and variation in best frequency with depth from each recording site to determine whether it was from the central nucleus or shell regions of IC (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C; Bulkin and Groh, 2011; Ress and Chandrasekaran, 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C and cited literature.

claim: IC units in both central and shell regions exhibited multiple response types to pure tone stimuli.
source: IC units in both regions exhibited multiple response types to pure tone stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Inhibited and offset responses were common in IC of awake animals.
source: In addition to excitatory responses (e.g., onset and sustained responses), inhibited and offset responses were common, as has previously been characterized in IC of awake animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E, top right, bottom middle; Duque and Malmierca, 2015).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and cited literature.

claim: Tuning curves from central regions were sharp and narrow, whereas units in shell regions exhibited broad frequency tuning.
source: Consistent with previous findings, tuning curves from central regions were sharp and narrow, whereas units in shell regions exhibited broad frequency tuning (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, left vs. right; Aitkin et al., 1975; Syka et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and cited literature.

claim: Inhibited side bands were common in tuning curves from both central and shell regions of IC.
source: Inhibited side bands were common in tuning curves from both regions, and some inhibited tuning curves were observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2G.

claim: The experimental parameters elicit sound responses and tuning properties characteristic of central and shell regions of the awake IC.
source: These data confirm that our experimental parameters elicit sound responses and tuning properties characteristic of central and shell regions of the awake IC (Aitkin et al., 1975; Duque and Malmierca, 2015; Syka et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: Much of the research regarding SSA and deviance detection in IC to date has been performed in anesthetized animals.
source: Much of the research regarding SSA and deviance detection in IC to date has been performed in anesthetized animals, with few studies recording from awake subjects (Duque and Malmierca, 2015; Parras et al., 2017).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature.

claim: Neuronal responses to sound depend on the state of anesthesia of the subject.
source: Given that neuronal responses to sound depend on the state of anesthesia of the subject, it is possible that there are differences in predictive coding metrics between the awake and anesthetized states (Fontanini and Katz, 2008; Gaese and Ostwald, 2001; Schumacher et al., 2011).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature.

claim: It remains unknown whether repetition and prediction metrics differ with anesthetic state.
source: While previous studies have characterized how anesthesia affects SSA, it remains unknown whether its component repetition and prediction metrics differ with anesthetic state (Duque and Malmierca, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: In the central IC, the mean iMM in the anesthetized condition was positive, indicative of prevalent adaptation.
source: In the central IC, the mean iMM in the anesthetized condition was positive, indicative of prevalent adaptation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 2B.

claim: The iMM values under anesthesia were significantly higher than those obtained while the animal was awake in central IC.
source: The iMM values under anesthesia were significantly higher than those obtained while the animal was awake (Figure 2B, Table 1; p=8.8e-05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 2B and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: In the anesthetized central IC, the mean iPE value of 0.077 indicated the presence of modest prediction error.
source: In the anesthetized condition, the mean iPE value of 0.077 indicated the presence of modest prediction error
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the anesthetized condition.

claim: A mean iPE of –0.13 indicated that negative prediction error is significantly more prevalent in the awake condition in central IC.
source: while a mean iPE of –0.13 indicated that negative prediction error is significantly more prevalent in the awake condition (Figure 2C, Table 1; p=0.017, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 2C and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Prominent repetition suppression was observed in the central IC under both anesthetized and awake conditions.
source: Under both anesthetized and awake conditions, prominent repetition suppression was observed in the central IC (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 2D.

claim: The mean iMM was significantly more positive in shell regions during anesthesia compared to awake.
source: Similar to the central IC, the mean iMM was significantly more positive in shell regions during anesthesia (Figure 2E, Table 1; p=3.5e-08, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 2E and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: A greater proportion of units in the awake condition had a negative iMM compared with the anesthetized distribution in shell IC.
source: A greater proportion of units in the awake condition had a negative iMM compared with the anesthetized distribution, indicating that facilitation (a greater response to the standard than the deviant context) is more common in the awake than the anesthetized condition (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2E.

claim: Facilitation is more common in the awake than the anesthetized condition in shell IC.
source: indicating that facilitation (a greater response to the standard than the deviant context) is more common in the awake than the anesthetized condition (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observation supported by Figure 2E.

claim: Prediction error is significantly higher in the awake compared to the anesthetized condition in shell IC.
source: The iPE values in shell IC suggest that prediction error is significantly higher in the awake compared to the anesthetized condition (Figure 2F, Table 1; p=2.6e-05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 2F and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: The distribution for the iRS under anesthesia in shell IC had a positive mean of 0.25, indicating prevalent repetition suppression.
source: Although the distribution for the iRS under anesthesia had a positive mean of 0.25, indicating prevalent repetition suppression
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the anesthetized condition.

claim: The awake distribution of iRS exhibited a significant leftward shift compared to anesthetized in shell IC.
source: the awake distribution exhibited a significant leftward shift by comparison (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2G.

claim: The mean iRS for the awake condition was negative (mean = −0.056), indicating that repetition enhancement is present in the awake shell IC.
source: Interestingly, the mean iRS for the awake condition was negative (mean = −0.056), indicating that repetition enhancement, rather than suppression, is present in the awake shell IC (Figure 2G, Table 1; p=2.5e-16, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 2G and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Repetition enhancement and negative prediction error are more prominent in awake animals.
source: These results point to differences between predictive coding metrics in the awake and anesthetized states, with previously undescribed metrics such as repetition enhancement and negative prediction error more prominent in awake animals.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings comparing awake and anesthetized states.

claim: The iMM for adapting units in the central nucleus significantly decreased with laser inactivation of cortico-collicular neurons.
source: The iMM for adapting units in the central nucleus significantly decreased with laser inactivation of cortico-collicular neurons (Figure 3D, top; Table 1; p=0.00034, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 3D and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: The iMM at baseline for adapting units in central IC predominantly represents repetition suppression and a small amount of prediction error.
source: The iMM at baseline for adapting units predominantly represents repetition suppression (Figure 3D, bottom) and a small amount of prediction error (Figure 3D, middle).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3D.

claim: Prediction error was abolished during laser inactivation in central IC adapting units.
source: Prediction error was abolished during laser inactivation (Figure 3D, middle; Table 1; p=0.048, Wilcoxon signed-rank test)
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 3D and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Repetition suppression remained unaffected during laser inactivation in central IC adapting units.
source: while repetition suppression remained unaffected (Figure 3D, bottom).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 3D.

claim: Adapting units in shell regions of IC exhibited a similar pattern to those in the central nucleus.
source: Adapting units in shell regions of IC exhibited a similar pattern to those in the central nucleus.
evidence: This is a summary statement comparing findings across IC regions.

claim: At baseline, shell IC adapting units encoded both prediction error and repetition suppression.
source: At baseline, these units encoded both prediction error and repetition suppression (Figure 3E, middle and bottom).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3E.

claim: A significant decrease in iMM during laser inactivation in shell IC adapting units was driven by a decrease in prediction error.
source: A significant decrease in iMM during laser inactivation (Figure 3E, top; Table 1; p=0.0023, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) was driven by a decrease in prediction error (Figure 3E, middle; Table 1; p=0.034, Wilcoxon signed-rank test)
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 3E and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Repetition suppression remained unaffected during laser inactivation in shell IC adapting units.
source: whereas repetition suppression remained unaffected (Figure 3E, bottom).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 3E.

claim: Removing cortical feedback reduced prediction error but not repetition suppression in adapting units.
source: Combined, these results suggest that removing cortical feedback reduced prediction error but not repetition suppression in adapting units.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings for adapting units.

claim: Prior studies of deviance detection in IC have focused exclusively on adapting units.
source: Prior studies of deviance detection in IC have focused exclusively on adapting units.
evidence: This is background information about previous research.

claim: Cortico-collicular inactivation led to a significant decrease in facilitation in facilitating units in the central nucleus.
source: In the central nucleus, cortico-collicular inactivation led to a significant decrease in facilitation in facilitating units (Figure 3G, top; Table 1; p=0.0036, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 3G and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: At baseline, the iMM for central IC facilitating units represents a combination of negative prediction error and repetition enhancement.
source: At baseline, the iMM for facilitating units represents a combination of negative prediction error and repetition enhancement (Figure 3G, middle and bottom).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3G.

claim: During inactivation, negative prediction error remained unaffected in central IC facilitating units.
source: During inactivation, negative prediction error remained unaffected (Figure 3G, middle)
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 3G.

claim: Repetition enhancement was nearly abolished during inactivation in central IC facilitating units.
source: while repetition enhancement was nearly abolished (Figure 3G, bottom; Table 1; p=0.0026, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 3G and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Facilitating units in the shell IC were significantly affected by cortico-collicular inactivation.
source: Facilitating units in the shell IC were also significantly affected by cortico-collicular inactivation (Figure 3H, top; Table 1; p=0.0016, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 3H and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: The change in iMM in shell IC facilitating units was driven by the near abolishment of negative prediction error.
source: In this case, however, the change in iMM was driven by the near abolishment of negative prediction error (Figure 3H, middle; Table 1; p=0.037, Wilcoxon signed-rank test)
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 3H and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Repetition enhancement was unaffected during inactivation in shell IC facilitating units.
source: while repetition enhancement was unaffected (Figure 3H, bottom).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 3H.

claim: Adaptation in the awake IC is composed of prediction error and repetition suppression.
source: These data suggest that adaptation and facilitation in the awake IC are composed of distinct underlying processes: adapting populations in both central and shell regions of IC exhibit prediction error and repetition suppression
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings for adapting units.

claim: Facilitation in the awake IC is characterized by negative prediction error and repetition enhancement.
source: while facilitating populations are characterized by negative prediction error and repetition enhancement.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings for facilitating units.

claim: In adapting units in both central and shell regions, cortico-collicular inactivation significantly decreases prediction error.
source: In adapting units in both central and shell regions, cortico-collicular inactivation significantly decreases prediction error.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings for adapting units.

claim: Facilitating units in the central IC display decreased repetition enhancement with cortico-collicular inactivation.
source: Facilitating units in the central IC display decreased repetition enhancement with cortico-collicular inactivation
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings for central facilitating units.

claim: Facilitating units in shell regions exhibit decreased negative prediction error with cortico-collicular inactivation.
source: while those in shell regions exhibit decreased negative prediction error.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings for shell facilitating units.

claim: Control experiments were performed in two mice with identical manipulations to the experimental group, but in the absence of ArchT.
source: To ensure that the laser-induced changes described above were opsin-mediated, we performed control experiments in two mice with identical manipulations to the experimental group, but in the absence of ArchT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological description of control experiments.

claim: At baseline, the control group exhibited a similar distribution of iMM values to the experimental group in both the central and shell regions of IC.
source: At baseline, the control group exhibited a similar distribution of iMM values to the experimental group in both the central and shell regions of IC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Table 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from control experiments supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Table 2.

claim: Similar proportions of adapting/facilitating/nonadapting units were found in the control and experimental groups.
source: Similar proportions of adapting/facilitating/nonadapting units were also found in the control (central: 23% adapting, 5% facilitating, 71% nonadapting; shell: 29% adapting, 18% facilitating, 53% nonadapting) and experimental groups (central: 24% adapting, 6% facilitating, 70% nonadapting; shell: 29% adapting, 9% facilitating, 62% nonadapting).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental and control data.

claim: No significant differences were found between baseline and laser trials for either adapting or facilitating units in either region in control experiments.
source: We found no significant differences between baseline and laser trials for either adapting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D, Table 2) or facilitating (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F) units in either region.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from control experiments supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Table 2.

claim: The observed effects of cortico-collicular inactivation were due to opsin-mediated inactivation of the cortico-collicular projection neurons.
source: This experiment confirmed that the observed effects of cortico-collicular inactivation were indeed due to opsin-mediated inactivation of the cortico-collicular projection neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the control experiment findings.

claim: The majority of units in both central and shell IC do not exhibit either adaptation or facilitation but respond similarly to tones when they are presented as a standard or deviant.
source: The majority of units in both central and shell IC do not exhibit either adaptation or facilitation but respond similarly to tones when they are presented as a standard or deviant (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Nonadapting units in the central nucleus exhibited a significant increase in iMM during inactivation.
source: Nonadapting units in the central nucleus exhibited a significant increase in iMM during inactivation (Figure 4C, top; Table 1; p=2.7e-06, Wilcoxon signed-rank test)
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 4C and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Nonadapting units in the shell IC were unaffected by inactivation.
source: whereas those in the shell IC were unaffected (Figure 4D, top).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 4D.

claim: The change in iMM for nonadapting units in the central nucleus was driven by a significant increase in iRS.
source: The change in iMM for nonadapting units in the central nucleus was driven by a significant increase in iRS (Figure 4C, bottom middle; Table 1; p=0.0011, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 4C and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Only central nonadapting units with negative baseline iRS values (showing repetition enhancement) were significantly affected by cortico-collicular inactivation.
source: Only those units with negative baseline iRS values (i.e., those units showing repetition enhancement) were significantly affected by cortico-collicular inactivation (Figure 4C, bottom; Table 1; p=0.00012, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 4C and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: In control experiments without ArchT, no significant changes were observed in nonadapting units.
source: In control experiments without ArchT, no significant changes were observed in nonadapting units (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H, Table 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from control experiments supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Table 2.

claim: Central nonadapting units display repetition enhancement, and input from the cortex is critical for expression of this phenomenon.
source: These results indicate that, similar to central facilitating units, central nonadapting units display repetition enhancement, and that input from the cortex is critical for expression of this phenomenon.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings for nonadapting units.

claim: Adapting units in the central nucleus increased responses to the standard and decreased responses to the deviant during inactivation.
source: We found that adapting units in the central nucleus increased responses to the standard (Figure 5A, Table 1; p=0.0092, one-sample t-test) and decreased responses to the deviant (Figure 5A, Table 1; p=0.0054, one-sample t-test) during inactivation.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 5A and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: The firing rate to the cascade stimulus did not change during cortico-collicular inactivation in central IC adapting units.
source: the firing rate to the cascade stimulus did not change during cortico-collicular inactivation
evidence: This is an experimental observation from Figure 5A.

claim: The decrease in firing rate to the deviant alone underlies the decrease in prediction error observed for central IC adapting units.
source: which means that the decrease in firing rate to the deviant alone underlies the decrease in prediction error observed for this population (Figure 3D, middle).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings linking changes in firing rates to changes in prediction error.

claim: Adapting units in the shell exhibited bidirectional changes to the standard and deviant, with no change in response to the cascade condition.
source: Adapting units in the shell exhibited the same pattern of bidirectional changes to the standard (Figure 5B, Table 1; p=0.035, one-sample Wilcoxon test) and deviant (Figure 5B, Table 1; p=0.0057, one-sample Wilcoxon test), similarly accounting for their decrease in iMM and prediction error (Figure 3E), with no change in response to the cascade condition (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 5B and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Inactivation of the cortico-collicular pathway induces bidirectional changes in firing rates to the standard and deviant for adapting units in both central and shell regions of IC.
source: These data suggest that inactivation of the cortico-collicular pathway induces bidirectional changes in firing rates to the standard and deviant for adapting units in both central and shell regions of IC.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings for adapting units.

claim: For central facilitating units, only the firing rate to the standard context changed during inactivation.
source: For central facilitating units, only the firing rate to the standard context changed during inactivation (Figure 5C, Table 1; p=0.0013, one-sample t-test)
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 5C and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: The change in firing rate to the standard context explains the observed change in repetition enhancement for central facilitating units.
source: explaining the observed change in repetition enhancement for this population (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings linking changes in firing rates to changes in repetition enhancement.

claim: For shell facilitating units, a decreased response to the standard and an increased response to the deviant were elicited on laser trials.
source: For shell facilitating units, a decreased response to the standard (Figure 5D, Table 1; p=0.0042, one-sample t-test) and an increased response to the deviant (Figure 5D, Table 1; p=0.0013, one-sample t-test) were elicited on laser trials
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 5D and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: The changes in firing rates for shell facilitating units account for changes in the iMM and the abolishment of negative prediction error.
source: accounting for changes in the iMM and the abolishment of negative prediction error (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings linking changes in firing rates to changes in iMM and negative prediction error.

claim: The firing rate changes for facilitating units are directionally opposite to those observed for adapting units under inactivation.
source: These changes are directionally opposite to the observed firing rate changes observed for adapting units under inactivation, with a decrease to the standard context for both central and shell units and an increase to the deviant context for shell units.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental findings across unit types.

claim: For nonadapting units, a significant decrease in response to the standard context was observed in both central and shell regions of IC.
source: For nonadapting units, a significant decrease in response to the standard context was observed in both central (Figure 5E, Table 1; p=1.4e-06, one-sample Wilcoxon test) and shell (Figure 5F, Table 1; p=0.035, one-sample Wilcoxon test) regions of IC.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 5E and F and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: The decrease in response to the standard was only significant enough to produce an effect on the iMM in central regions for nonadapting units.
source: The decrease was only significant enough to produce an effect on the iMM in central regions (Figure 4C, top), leading to an increase in repetition suppression (Figure 4C, bottom).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings for nonadapting units.

claim: For adapting and facilitating units, IC responses to the standard and deviant contexts in the absence of cortical input are bidirectionally modulated, such that neurons respond more similarly to both contexts.
source: For adapting and facilitating units, these data exhibit that IC responses to the standard and deviant contexts in the absence of cortical input are bidirectionally modulated, such that neurons respond more similarly to both contexts rather than firing differentially to each.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings for adapting and facilitating units.

claim: For nonadapting units, the response to the standard context alone is diminished during cortico-collicular inactivation, causing these units to become more adapting.
source: For nonadapting units, the response to the standard context alone is diminished during cortico-collicular inactivation, causing these units to become more adapting.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings for nonadapting units.

claim: Under normal conditions AC provides information regarding sound context to neurons in IC.
source: These changes suggest that under normal conditions AC provides information regarding sound context to neurons in IC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Both the adapting and nonadapting groups in the central IC contained units with significant values for both iPE and iRS, most often resulting from a combination of negative prediction error and repetition suppression.
source: Both the adapting and nonadapting groups in the central IC contained units with significant values for both iPE and iRS, most often resulting from a combination of negative prediction error and repetition suppression (Figure 6A, maroon dots).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 6A.

claim: In the shell IC, a greater variety of response combinations was observed compared to central IC.
source: In the shell IC, a greater variety of response combinations was observed.
evidence: This is an experimental observation comparing central and shell IC.

claim: All three groups in shell IC contained units with both significant negative prediction error and repetition suppression, as well as a separate population exhibiting significant prediction error and repetition enhancement.
source: All three groups contained units with both significant negative prediction error and repetition suppression, as well as a separate population exhibiting significant prediction error and repetition enhancement (Figure 6B, maroon dots).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 6B.

claim: Some shell adapting units exhibited a combination of both repetition suppression and prediction error.
source: Some shell adapting units also exhibited a combination of both repetition suppression and prediction error (Figure 6B, left).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 6B.

claim: Units in IC exhibit distinct combinations of repetition suppression/enhancement and prediction error/negative prediction error.
source: These results suggest that the units in IC exhibit distinct combinations of repetition suppression/enhancement and prediction error/negative prediction error.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations of iPE and iRS combinations.

claim: Facilitating units in both central and shell regions of IC exhibited repetition enhancement at baseline.
source: Facilitating units in both central and shell regions of IC exhibited repetition enhancement at baseline, as defined by the difference in firing rate to the last standard and the same tone embedded in the cascade sequence (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3G and H.

claim: The progression of standards by position exhibited subsequent enhancements in firing rate that was plateaued by the second to last standard before the deviant for both central and shell facilitating units.
source: The progression of standards by position exhibited subsequent enhancements in firing rate that was plateaued by the second to last standard before the deviant for both central (Figure 6C) and shell facilitating units (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 6C and D.

claim: The firing rate to the last standard was significantly higher than the first in both central and shell facilitating units.
source: The firing rate to the last standard was significantly higher than the first in both regions (Figure 6C, Table 1; p=0.0017, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 6D, Table 1; p=9.3e-05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 6C and D and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Facilitating units in IC exhibit true repetition enhancement.
source: These data provide evidence that facilitating units in IC exhibit true repetition enhancement.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings showing sequential increases in firing rate.

claim: AC is critically involved in regulating both repetition and prediction effects in the awake IC.
source: The results of this study indicate that AC is critically involved in regulating both repetition and prediction effects in the awake IC, providing evidence for the implementation of predictive coding in cortico-subcortical networks.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study stated in the Discussion.

claim: The study provides evidence for the implementation of predictive coding in cortico-subcortical networks.
source: The results of this study indicate that AC is critically involved in regulating both repetition and prediction effects in the awake IC, providing evidence for the implementation of predictive coding in cortico-subcortical networks.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study stated in the Discussion.

claim: Adapting and facilitating units were bidirectionally modulated by cortico-collicular inactivation.
source: Adapting and facilitating units were bidirectionally modulated by cortico-collicular inactivation, with adapting units becoming less adapting and facilitating units becoming less facilitating on laser trials (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 3.

claim: The decrease in adaptation for adapting units was driven by a decrease in prediction error for units in both central and shell regions of IC.
source: The decrease in adaptation for adapting units was driven by a decrease in prediction error for units in both central and shell regions of IC ( Figure 3D, Figure 5E, Figure 7, pink arrows).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings stated in the Discussion and supported by Figures 3D, 5E, and 7.

claim: For facilitating and nonadapting units in the central nucleus, inactivation-driven changes were caused by a decrease in repetition enhancement.
source: For facilitating and nonadapting units in the central nucleus, inactivation-driven changes were caused by a decrease in repetition enhancement (Figure 3G, Figure 7, gold dashed arrows).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings stated in the Discussion and supported by Figures 3G and 7.

claim: The decrease in facilitation in the shell IC was caused by the abolishment of negative prediction error.
source: The decrease in facilitation in the shell IC, however, was caused by the abolishment of negative prediction error (Figure 3H, Figure 7, pink dashed arrows).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings stated in the Discussion and supported by Figures 3H and 7.

claim: In adapting units, changes were modulated by an increased response to the standard and decreased response to the deviant.
source: In adapting units, these changes were modulated by an increased response to the standard and decreased response to the deviant, while the opposite pattern was true for facilitating units (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 5.

claim: The opposite pattern of firing rate changes was true for facilitating units compared to adapting units.
source: In adapting units, these changes were modulated by an increased response to the standard and decreased response to the deviant, while the opposite pattern was true for facilitating units (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 5.

claim: Without input from AC, IC responds more similarly to tones in the standard and deviant contexts.
source: Overall, these bidirectional changes indicate that, without input from AC, IC responds more similarly to tones in the standard and deviant contexts.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: AC provides critical contextual cues about the statistics of the auditory environment to targets in IC under normal conditions.
source: These findings demonstrate that AC provides critical contextual cues about the statistics of the auditory environment to targets in IC under normal conditions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The iMM values in the awake and anesthetized brain reflect different underlying processes.
source: These findings suggest that the iMM values in the awake and anesthetized brain reflect different underlying processes, and that anesthesia induces bidirectional changes in metrics of repetition and prediction.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental findings comparing awake and anesthetized states.

claim: Anesthesia induces bidirectional changes in metrics of repetition and prediction.
source: These findings suggest that the iMM values in the awake and anesthetized brain reflect different underlying processes, and that anesthesia induces bidirectional changes in metrics of repetition and prediction.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental findings comparing awake and anesthetized states.

claim: Previous studies that have applied a predictive coding framework to decompose neuronal mismatch have focused exclusively on adapting neurons.
source: Because previous studies that have applied a predictive coding framework to decompose neuronal mismatch have focused exclusively on adapting neurons, the repetition enhancement found here in facilitating units has not been previously described (Parras et al., 2017).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: The repetition enhancement found in facilitating units has not been previously described in the context of predictive coding in IC.
source: Because previous studies that have applied a predictive coding framework to decompose neuronal mismatch have focused exclusively on adapting neurons, the repetition enhancement found here in facilitating units has not been previously described (Parras et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding in the Discussion.

claim: Repetition enhancement is a common phenomenon in humans, existing either alongside or in place of repetition suppression.
source: However, it is well-documented in fMRI literature that repetition enhancement is a common phenomenon in humans, existing either alongside or in place of repetition suppression (de Gardelle et al., 2013; Müller et al., 2013; Segaert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: Repetition enhancement has been proposed to reflect novel network formation and consolidation of novel sensory representations.
source: Interestingly, repetition enhancement has been proposed to reflect novel network formation and consolidation of novel sensory representations (Segaert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature cited in the Discussion.

claim: Once new representations have been formed, repetition suppression is hypothesized to take over, reflecting the minimization in prediction errors.
source: Once new representations have been formed, repetition suppression is hypothesized to take over, reflecting the minimization in prediction errors that occurs when new representations give rise to accurate predictions (Auksztulewicz and Friston, 2016; de Gardelle et al., 2013; Friston and Kiebel, 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature cited in the Discussion.

claim: Repetition enhancement has been observed in the MGB in response to temporally degraded stimuli.
source: Repetition enhancement has also been observed in the MGB in response to temporally degraded stimuli that are hypothesized to engage top-down resources to compensate for bottom-up acoustic information loss (Cai et al., 2016; Kommajosyula et al., 2019).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: Repetition enhancement in MGB is reversed when cortico-thalamic pathways are blocked.
source: Interestingly, this enhancement is reversed when cortico-thalamic pathways are blocked, further suggesting that repetition enhancement in the auditory system reflects a top-down phenomenon (Kommajosyula et al., 2021).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: Repetition suppression can be viewed from the perspective of neuronal fatigue, whereby the incremental decrease in firing rate to a repeated standard tone is explained by synaptic depression.
source: While repetition suppression can be understood from a predictive coding framework, it can also be viewed from the perspective of neuronal fatigue, whereby the incremental decrease in firing rate to a repeated standard tone is simply explained by synaptic depression (Escera and Malmierca, 2014; Taaseh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: The processes that underlie repetition suppression in IC do not involve top-down cortical signals.
source: While these data do not provide definitive proof of either perspective, they do suggest that the processes that underlie repetition suppression in IC do not involve top-down cortical signals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings stated in the Discussion.

claim: Repetition suppression was much more prevalent when animals were under anesthesia, a state in which the auditory responsiveness in the cortex is compromised.
source: This notion is supported by the fact that repetition suppression was much more prevalent when animals were under anesthesia, a state in which the auditory responsiveness in the cortex is compromised (Figure 2G; Brugge and Merzenich, 1973; Katsuki et al., 1959).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 2G and cited literature.

claim: According to models of hierarchical predictive coding, higher-order stations generate predictions that they broadcast to lower centers.
source: According to models of hierarchical predictive coding, higher-order stations generate predictions that they broadcast to lower centers (Friston and Kiebel, 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: Predictions are compared with representations of the actual sensory input, and if there is a mismatch, a prediction error is generated and forwarded up the hierarchy.
source: These predictions are compared with representations of the actual sensory input, and if there is a mismatch, a prediction error is generated and forwarded up the hierarchy (Friston and Kiebel, 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: Under the hierarchical predictive coding framework, the inactivation of top-down inputs would interfere with communication of predictions, leading to dysfunction in the prediction error response.
source: Under this framework, the inactivation of top-down inputs would interfere with communication of predictions, leading to dysfunction in the prediction error response, as seen in our data.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings in the context of predictive coding theory stated in the Discussion.

claim: Another possibility is that prediction errors are directly backpropagated from AC to IC.
source: Another possibility is that prediction errors are directly backpropagated from AC to IC.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis stated in the Discussion.

claim: Evidence for prediction error has been found in deep layers of the cortex in which feedback neurons reside.
source: While this contradicts canonical predictive coding models, evidence for prediction error has been found in deep layers of the cortex in which feedback neurons reside (Asilador and Llano, 2020; Rummell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: Feedback from AC plays a critical role in the generation of prediction error in IC.
source: Though the precise mechanism underlying the generation of prediction error in IC remains unclear, our data show that feedback from AC plays a critical role in this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: A stronger response to a tone in the cascade sequence compared to the context in which it is a deviant could simply reflect a relative lack of cross-frequency adaptation.
source: A stronger response to a tone in the cascade sequence compared to the context in which it is a deviant could simply reflect a relative lack of cross-frequency adaptation
evidence: This is an alternative explanation for negative prediction error stated in the Discussion.

claim: Previous studies have found that cross-frequency adaptation occurs between channels with a frequency separation of a third of an octave or less.
source: Previous studies that have investigated the effective bandwidth for cross-frequency adaptation, however, have found that it occurs between channels with a frequency separation of a third of an octave or less (Taaseh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: The stimuli used in this study had a half-octave frequency separation, indicating that cross-frequency effects should be minimized.
source: The stimuli used in this study had a half-octave frequency separation, indicating that cross-frequency effects should be minimized.
evidence: This is a methodological detail stated in the Discussion to support the interpretation of negative prediction error.

claim: It is unlikely that the negative prediction error responses observed in this study simply reflect cross-frequency adaptation to the oddball stimulus.
source: Therefore, it is unlikely that the negative prediction error responses observed in this study simply reflect cross-frequency adaptation to the oddball stimulus.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the stimulus parameters.

claim: A stronger response to a tone when it is embedded in a completely predictable sequence than when it is a deviant could signify that a neuron encodes predictions, rather than prediction errors.
source: A stronger response to a tone when it is embedded in a completely predictable sequence, such as the cascade sequence, than when it is a deviant could also signify that a neuron encodes predictions, rather than prediction errors.
evidence: This is an interpretation of negative prediction error stated in the Discussion.

claim: In hierarchical predictive coding, both predictions and prediction errors are generated at every level of the hierarchy.
source: In hierarchical predictive coding, both predictions and prediction errors are generated at every level of the hierarchy, with prediction errors being forwarded to ascending sensory centers and predictions being backpropagated (Friston and Kiebel, 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: In the shell IC, evidence for negative prediction error was abolished during cortico-collicular inactivation, consistent with the notion that feedback from the cortex may carry predictions to IC.
source: In the shell IC, the region that receives the vast majority of descending cortical input, evidence for negative prediction error was abolished during cortico-collicular inactivation (Figure 3H), consistent with the notion that feedback from the cortex may carry predictions to IC (Bajo et al., 2007; Herbert et al., 1991; Saldaña et al., 1996; Stebbings et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 3H and cited literature.

claim: Negative prediction error in the central nucleus remained unperturbed during inactivation of cortical feedback.
source: Interestingly, negative prediction error in the central nucleus remained unperturbed during inactivation of cortical feedback (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is an experimental finding stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 3G.

claim: Only a small fraction of cortico-collicular fibers terminate in the central nucleus.
source: Given that only a small fraction of cortico-collicular fibers terminate in the central nucleus, it is likely that it receives predictions from another source (Bajo et al., 2007; Herbert et al., 1991; Saldaña et al., 1996; Stebbings et al., 2014).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: The central nucleus likely receives predictions from another source besides AC.
source: Given that only a small fraction of cortico-collicular fibers terminate in the central nucleus, it is likely that it receives predictions from another source (Bajo et al., 2007; Herbert et al., 1991; Saldaña et al., 1996; Stebbings et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the Discussion based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: An intriguing potential candidate for the source of predictions to central IC could be the shell IC.
source: An intriguing potential candidate for this source of predictions could be the shell IC, given the extensive network of intracollicular connections in IC (Lesicko et al., 2020; Saldaña and Merchán, 1992; Saldaña and Merchán, 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the Discussion based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: Laser inactivation achieved only partial and not complete inactivation of the cortico-collicular pathway.
source: One limitation of this study is that laser inactivation achieved only partial and not complete inactivation of the cortico-collicular pathway.
evidence: This is a limitation stated in the Discussion.

claim: Light itself can have a modulatory or toxic effect on neurons.
source: Given that light itself can have a modulatory or toxic effect on neurons, these types of optogenetic experiments require a careful titration between using enough power to substantially affect the population of interest without causing nonspecific light or heat-based perturbations (Tyssowski and Gray, 2019).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: Other techniques, such as chemogenetic approaches or cooling, provide more complete inactivation but do not allow for rapid and reversible inactivation.
source: Though other techniques, such as chemogenetic approaches or cooling, provide more complete inactivation, they do not allow for rapid and reversible inactivation (English and Roth, 2015).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: The reduction in firing achieved with the laser power parameters produced clear effects on repetition and prediction processing in IC.
source: With our laser power parameters, we found a mean 60% reduction in firing in putative cortico-collicular neurons at baseline and a 45% reduction during presentation of pure tone stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D). This reduction produced clear effects on repetition and prediction processing in IC, in several cases with the severe reduction or complete abolishment of certain metrics of deviance detection, such as prediction error and repetition enhancement in the central nucleus and negative prediction error in the shell IC (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion to justify the partial inactivation approach and supported by Figures 1—figure supplement 1D and 3.

claim: The results should be interpreted bearing in mind that they reflect only partial and not complete inactivation.
source: The interpretation of these results should bear in mind that they reflect only partial and not complete inactivation.
evidence: This is a caveat stated in the Discussion.

claim: No differences were observed in the iMM distribution between single- and multiunits.
source: Although we observed no differences in the iMM distribution between single- and multiunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The results should be interpreted with the limitation that analyses were performed on pooled single- and multiunit data.
source: the results of this study should be interpreted with this limitation in mind, namely, photosuppression-induced changes in these units may not reflect changes in single neurons.
evidence: This is a caveat stated in the Discussion.

claim: Cortico-collicular neurons are known to branch to additional subcortical targets besides the IC.
source: Whereas this study focuses on changes specific to the cortico-collicular pathway, it should be noted that cortico-collicular neurons are known to branch to additional subcortical targets besides the IC, including the MGB, caudal regions of the dorsal striatum, and the lateral amygdala (Asokan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is background information cited from previous literature stated in the Discussion.

claim: The photo-suppression experiments produce short-latency effects in the IC, indicating that the observed changes are likely due to direct, monosynaptic AC to IC pathways.
source: The fact that our photo-suppression experiments produce short-latency effects in the IC (Figure 3C and F) indicates that the observed changes are likely due to direct, monosynaptic AC to IC pathways, and that multisynaptic effects from other collateral sites are unlikely.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 3C and F.

claim: The potential contribution from additional downstream targets of cortico-collicular neurons cannot be definitely ruled out.
source: Nevertheless, the potential contribution from these additional downstream targets cannot be definitely ruled out and should be factored into the interpretation of the results.
evidence: This is a caveat stated in the Discussion.

claim: Deviance detection and predictive coding in IC involve additional complexity than has been previously described.
source: Our findings indicate that deviance detection and predictive coding in IC involve additional complexity than has been previously described.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: This study provides the first description of facilitating units in IC.
source: We provide here the first description of facilitating units in IC, as well as evidence for the existence of repetition enhancement and negative prediction error in these units.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution in the Discussion.

claim: This study provides evidence for the existence of repetition enhancement and negative prediction error in facilitating units in IC.
source: We provide here the first description of facilitating units in IC, as well as evidence for the existence of repetition enhancement and negative prediction error in these units.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution in the Discussion.

claim: AC is involved in the generation of prediction error in IC.
source: We show that AC regulates these metrics and is also involved in the generation of prediction error in IC.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: Repetition suppression is unaffected by inactivation of cortical input to IC, providing evidence that this process may reflect bottom-up fatigue rather than top-down predictive processing.
source: Repetition suppression is unaffected by inactivation of cortical input to IC, providing evidence that this process may reflect bottom-up fatigue rather than top-down predictive processing.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: The results demonstrate the role of AC in providing contextual cues about the auditory stream to targets in IC.
source: These results demonstrate the role of AC in providing contextual cues about the auditory stream to targets in IC.
evidence: This is the final summary conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: Experiments were performed in six adult Cdh23 mice (four males and two females, age 3–8 months).
source: We performed experiments in six adult Cdh23 mice (Cdh23tm2.1Kjn/J, RRID:IMSR_JAX:018399; four males and two females, age 3–8 months).
